slides.title: Why your DTF transfers *crack* or feel thick
slides.sub: Too much ink in one spot. Three RIP settings decide how much lands there.

slides.label: Ink one dark pixel can get with no limit
slides.note: Plus 100% white underneath. Five layers of wet ink that never fully dry before the powder.

slides.label: The total ink limit range on DTF film
slides.note: The limit caps the sum of C + M + Y + K on one spot. The printer will not stop by itself. The RIP must.

items.d: Swaps the gray part of a color (equal C, M and Y) for black ink.
Less total ink for the same color, sharper dark detail, a thinner film.
60% is a safe default. Use 80% for designs with heavy dark shading.

items.t: Start at C 80 · M 80 · Y 70 · K 70
items.d: Past this point more drops only make the ink wetter, not darker.
Lower that one channel by 10%.
Total ink limit too high. Drop it to 250%.
Ink limit and white both too high. Try 260% and 80% white.
Per-channel limits too high. Lower them by 10%.
GCR too high. Bring it down to 40–50%.

slides.title: Change one setting, print the same swatch
slides.body: Total ink limit and Black generation (GCR) are sliders in the RIP. Job history keeps every print with its settings, so you can go back to the one that worked.

slides.line: Total ink limit, GCR and per-channel limits in one RIP.

caption:
Your DTF transfer cracks after ten washes? That is too much ink in one spot.

With no limit, one dark pixel can get 400% ink plus a full white base. Cap it with a total ink limit of 250–280%, set black generation (GCR) to 60–80%, and trim per-channel limits if solids puddle. Change one setting at a time.

slides.title: Lines in your DTF prints? *6 causes*, in order
slides.sub: Check them in the wrong order and you waste film. This order finds it fastest.

slides.label: of banding is clogged nozzles
slides.note: Print a nozzle check on a strip of film. Any gap is a missing nozzle and a light line on every pass.

items.d: One or two cleanings usually fix it. White nozzles need the most care.
Alternating lines? Turn bidirectional off. If they vanish, set head gap 1–3.
At 720 × 720 each nozzle's error shows. More passes hide it.
Even lines one head pass wide: the film advanced too much or too little.
Lines get worse late in a long print: low tanks, air in a tube, old dampers.
View the file at 200%. If the bands are in the file, the printer is innocent.

slides.title: Print the channel test
slides.body: It shows every channel on its own. You see at once if the problem was one color or all of them.

slides.title: Where the checks live
slides.body: Maintenance → Nozzle check prints the pattern on film. Bidirectional and Head gap (bidi) are in the Printer tab.

slides.line: Nozzle check, channel test and bidirectional control in one RIP.

caption:
Fine lines across your DTF print? It looks like one problem. It has six causes.

Check in this order: clogged nozzles (70% of banding), bidirectional timing, too few passes, media feed, ink starvation, then the file itself. Print a channel test after any fix to see if it was one color or all of them.

slides.title: Dull, washed-out DTF colors? *Check in order*
slides.sub: Seven causes cover most of it. The first ones cost nothing to check.

slides.title: One swatch that splits the causes
slides.body: Solid C, M, Y, K, a gray ramp, a skin tone. Press on a black and a white shirt. Dull on both: the color layer. Dull only on black: the white.

items.d: Photoshop converts, then the RIP converts again. Keep sRGB. Convert once.
A profile made for another print mode gives blue grays and greenish browns.
Film looks dry and pale? Raise per-channel limits in 10% steps.
A dead yellow turns black purple. Run the channel test and a nozzle check.
Dull only on dark shirts? Use 100% white density and 10% highlight white.
Darks flat and grayish? Lower GCR from 60% to 40–50%.

slides.title: Cause 7: the finish and the screen

items.d: Neon greens and electric blues are outside what CMYK ink can print.
Parchment gives a matte finish. A Teflon sheet leaves a slight sheen.

slides.title: Logo turns pink overnight on polyester?
slides.body: That is dye migration from the fabric. No color setting fixes it. See the polyester guide: lower heat, dense white base.

slides.line: ZoroPrint: one conversion, per-channel limits, a white layer you tune.

caption:
Colors fine on screen, flat on the shirt? It is the most common DTF complaint.

Check in order: double conversion, the wrong profile, ink limits too low, a weak channel, thin white, too much black generation, then the finish. Start with one swatch pressed on a black and a white shirt. Change one setting at a time.

Full guide → zoroprint.com/guides/dull-washed-out-dtf-colors

slides.title: Keep your white ink *alive*
slides.sub: Converted Epsons fail from standing still, not from printing. Daily, weekly, monthly.

slides.label: Longest idle time without a short white print
slides.note: White ink is titanium dioxide in suspension. Left alone, it settles, thickens and dries in the nozzles.

items.d: Tanks or cartridges about 30 s. No hard shaking: it makes bubbles.
Fresh ink through every channel. Problems show before a customer job does.

items.t: Clean only if you see gaps
items.d: Chained cleanings waste ink and pull air into the lines.

items.t: Swab cap and wiper at close
items.d: Cleaning fluid on a foam swab: the cap lip and both sides of the wiper.
Dried white on the cap seal is the top cause of 'it was fine yesterday'.
A gummy wiper drags dried ink across the nozzle plate.
A clear band at the top means settling. Rock the tank, run a strip.
Low ink lets air in. Air is much harder to remove than a clog.
Flush the white lines with cleaning fluid and refill.
Air bubbles or discolored filters? Replace white dampers every 1–3 months.
A full waste pad stops the printer without warning.

left.label: Don't
items: Leave white in the head 10 days
Cut the power to the printer

right.label: Do
items: Or flush white, leave cleaner in lines
Keep power on for timer cleaning

slides.title: Let the RIP run the daily strip
slides.body: Maintenance → Add purge strip as the first job. 'Keep white ink moving while idle' prints a small white strip now and then, with film loaded.

slides.line: Purge strip, nozzle check and idle keep-alive built into the RIP.

caption:
Your printer "suddenly stopped printing white"? It skipped the routine.

White DTF ink settles, thickens and dries when it sits. Rock the white daily, print a purge strip first, clean only when you see gaps, and never leave it idle more than 2–3 days. Keep the room at 45–60% humidity: dry air causes most winter clogs.

Full guide → zoroprint.com/guides/white-ink-care-epson

slides.title: What makes one easy to convert

items.d: DTF color needs only 4 inks. Photo Epsons have 2 more for white.
Color and white can print in one pass.

items.t: A RIP that sends raw commands
items.d: Not the Epson driver. The RIP must drive the head directly.
White in the cyan + magenta tanks. The L800 is USB only.
Same layout as the L805, wider carriage, roll film. The most converted.
Same head family as the L1800. White in light cyan + light magenta.
One printer, two names. White in photo black + gray. Validated Sept 2026.

left.label: Experimental
items: Expect to adjust a setting or two

items.d: Newer 180-nozzle successors of the L805 and the L1800.
The A4 siblings of the ET-8550 and the L8180.
White in the red + gray tanks. Head offsets still being confirmed.
Premium 10-channel heads, white in the light channels.
Hoson, Senyang and BYHX boards use their own protocol, not ESC/P2.

items.t: On our list, no date yet

items.d: An A4 L805. Logos, patches and small gang sheets.
An A3+ L1800. Best known, so kits and help are easy to find.
The ET-8550 or L8180.

slides.line: Run the channel test on film once. It confirms your tank layout.

slides.title: White logo turned *pink* overnight?
slides.sub: That is dye migration. Four things stop it: heat, time, powder and the white layer.

slides.label: Where polyester dyes turn back into gas
slides.note: Press at the usual 160 °C and that gas moves into your white ink. Perfect off the press, pink by morning.

slides.label: For 10–12 s, light pressure, on polyester
slides.note: Every 10 °C below 160 halves the migration. Do not add time to compensate: time is exposure.

items.d: Melts at about 100–110 °C, so you can press cooler.
Adds a thin barrier layer. Worth it on red, black and neon polyester.
The press should only re-melt the powder, not cure it.
Even on light shirts. A dense base stops dye reaching the color layer.
Keep it there on polyester.
On polyester, never thin the white under dark colors.

left.label: The problem
items: A shiny rectangle around the design
Fibers flattened by heat and pressure

slides.title: Press, wait 24 hours, then look
slides.body: Test on the sleeve. Dye migration is slow. A test you judge straight off the press tells you nothing.

slides.line: White density and highlight white, tuned in ZoroPrint.

caption:
White logo perfect off the press, pink by morning? That is dye migration.

Polyester dyes turn back into gas around 160 °C. Press at 140–150 °C for 10–12 s, use low-temperature powder and anti-migration film, and run white density at 100%. Then test on a sleeve and wait 24 hours before you judge.
